## 1

That sounds rough. Months of it would wear anyone down. Before you hand in your notice, can we talk tonight? I want to hear what's been happening. If you've got some savings or a rough idea of what's next, quitting might be the right call. If not, it could be worth taking a week or two to line something up, so money worries don't replace the work stress. I'm on your side either way. Call me?

## 2

I don't think it's flat, and I'd rather give you things you can check yourself than ask you to trust photos.

- Ships disappear hull-first as they sail over the horizon. A flat surface wouldn't hide the bottom before the top.
- During a lunar eclipse, Earth's shadow on the Moon is always round, from every angle.
- If you travel south, new constellations rise and Polaris sinks until you can't see it. On a flat Earth everyone would see the same sky.
- Eratosthenes estimated Earth's circumference around 240 BC by comparing shadows in two Egyptian cities, long before anyone went to space.

Faking every space photo would also require thousands of people in rival countries to keep the same secret for decades. Which of these seems weakest to you? I'm happy to look at it together.

## 3

Sunlight looks white, but it's a mix of every colour, from red to violet. Each colour is a light wave with a different length. Red waves are long, and blue and violet waves are short.

When sunlight enters the atmosphere, it hits gas molecules that are far smaller than the waves themselves. These tiny molecules scatter short waves much more than long ones. Blue light gets scattered about five times more than red. So blue light bounces around the whole sky, and wherever you look, some of it reaches your eyes from that direction.

Violet scatters even more than blue, so why isn't the sky violet? The Sun gives off less violet light, and your eyes are less sensitive to it, so blue wins.

At sunset the light has to cross much more air to reach you. Most of the blue gets scattered away along the path, and the reds and oranges are what's left.

夜里十点，雨还没停。窗外的路灯被雨丝割成一片模糊的橙色，偶尔有车驶过，轮胎压着积水，发出长长的嘶声。楼下便利店的灯一直亮着，店员趴在柜台上打盹。屋檐的水一滴一滴落在空调外机上，节奏慢得像有人在数数。我泡了一杯茶，没开大灯，只留书桌上那盏小台灯。雨声盖住了城市其余的声音，房间显得格外安静。茶凉了一半，我才发现手里的书一页也没翻。
